newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe/Malaysia power deal faces criticism.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe/Malaysia power deal faces criticism.

text.p: Zimbabwe's state-owned power utility is seeking government cancellation of a privatisation deal signed last week with Malaysia, saying it was contrary to the country's efforts to economically empower the majority black population.
The independent Financial Gazette newspaper quoted Zimbabwe Electricity Supply Authority (ZESA) chairman Solomon Tawengwa as saying the government had not informed the authority of the deal.

The two countries signed a letter of intent last week under which Malaysian power producer YTL Corp Bhd would invest Z$6 billion (U.S.$580 million) in the privatisation of ZESA's Hwange Power Station in northern Zimbabwe.

"This (Malaysian) proposal does not empower indigenous (black) Zimbabweans in terms of the Zimbabwean indigenisation policy," the Financial Gazette quoted Tawengwa as saying in a letter he wrote to President Robert Mugabe.

"Hwange Power Station is of strategic importance to ZESA and is a prime asset. YTL's proposal in its current format is likely to have far-reaching adverse effects on ZESA's operations, the more obvious one being an inevitable increase in electricity tariffs," he said.
Tawengwa -- who was last week elected executive mayor of the capital Harare on the ruling ZANU-PF ticket -- and ZESA and energy ministry officials were unavailable for comment.
According to the Financial Gazette, Tawengwa queried the government's departure from an earlier decision to put out to tender a planned expansion of Hwange Thermal Power Station.

ZESA had invited bids for this project and a total of 19 companies had submitted tenders but only six were shortlisted with YTL at the bottom of the rankings after National Power of Britain and other European and American firms.

"The Board observed with concern that the manner in which the (Malaysian) Letter of Intent had been developed, signed and submitted to the board represented a fundamental departure from the course of action which the board and (the) government had been following," Tawengwa is quoted as saying.

"The contents of the Letter of Intent of September 15 were a serious contradiction to the guidelines in the 21st May, 1996 letter with respect to the competitive bidding process, the share ownership structure of the joint venture partnership and issues pertaining to government policy on indigenisation," he added.
